# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Restatement

This follow-up reports 24-month outcomes from two sources.

**Varden case-processing offices** (7 treated, 7 control; schedules kept for two years)

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2) |
| Hours, timesheets | −12% |
| Hours, new system-log measure | −11% |
| Per-hour gain, timesheets | +9.8%, down from +12.5% at nine months |
| Per-hour gain, logs | +8.5% (95% CI 3.4 to 13.8) |
| Quality | Unchanged |
| Sick days | −27% |
| Resignations | Still lower |

- **Mediation analysis**, registered at month 11: reduced meetings account for 47% of the per-hour gain, fatigue for 18%, and 35% is unexplained.
- **Meeting audit**: in month 15, two control offices cut meetings on their own initiative. Their output per hour then rose 4.1% against their own prior period.
- **Counter arm**: the county ended it at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and restoring service was estimated to need 12% more staff at about 9% more cost per contact.

**Halden subset** (14 of the 23 organisations with output records)

- Three reverted, with output indices of 88–91 at the time: a hospitality group and a retail chain citing coverage, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines.
- The 11 that continued show record-based output of 96.8 and hours down 13.4%, a gain of 11.8% per hour. The authors present this as a favourable, self-selected figure.

**The authors' conclusions**

- **Against Varga & Holm:** a gain survives the standards Varga & Holm recommended, so the gains are not entirely an artifact.
- **Against the meta-analysis:** its four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they cannot speak to decay. The one controlled long study shows the gain declining.

# Assessment

This report does what the earlier papers left undone, and its arithmetic holds:

- 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%, and 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%.
- 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%, and 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%.
- The mediation shares sum to 100%.
- The 3.3-hour difference in meeting time persists from nine months to 24 months.

It also tests decay within a single study, puts the meetings hypothesis to a registered test, adds a second hours measure, and reports the counter arm's termination plainly. Its verdicts on Varga & Holm and on the meta-analysis are fair, and it confirms the duration problem I raised about the meta-analysis.

The points below concern how strongly some findings are stated, plus one possible bias that runs through the decay result.

## Points worth addressing

**1. The summary's "12.5% → 8.5%" compares two different measures, and the decline itself isn't tested.**
- 12.5% comes from timesheets. 8.5% comes from logs. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%, which the Results section uses correctly.
- That is a fall of about a fifth. Section 5 calls it "about a quarter", which overstates it slightly.
- The two confidence intervals overlap substantially. The report needs a test of the *change* between nine and 24 months, taken within offices.
- What is well supported: the gain did not disappear. What is not yet established: that it declined, which may be noise.
- "Consistent with some fading" is fair wording. "The gain has therefore declined" states more than the evidence shows.

**2. The meeting audit contaminated the control arm, which biases the apparent decline upward.**
- From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings. If that raised their productivity, as the report suggests, the treated–control gap would narrow even if treated offices did not change at all.
- Part of the drop from 12.5% to 9.8% could therefore be the control arm improving rather than treated offices fading.
- To separate these, the report should:
  - show treated and control trajectories separately against their own baselines;
  - re-estimate the 24-month effect excluding the two audit offices, or censoring them at month 15.
- The audit itself can also be analysed more cleanly. The other five control offices over the same months give a better comparison than the audit offices' own previous six months.
- A reconciliation question: if the two audit offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, a control average of 7.2 → 7.0 implies the other five rose by about half an hour each. Is that what happened?

**3. What does log-in time on the case system actually measure?**
- If it records time spent on cases, it probably excludes meetings, email and other work off the system. In that case it measures a different quantity from timesheet hours, not a stricter version of the same one.
- That changes three things:
  - **The hours comparison.** −11% on logs against −12% on timesheets would be what you'd expect if freed meeting time moved into case work. It would not show that staff did "slightly more work" than they recorded.
  - **The outcome.** Output per log hour would mean output per hour spent on cases.
  - **The mediation result.** If meetings are outside the denominator, cutting them cannot raise output per log hour simply by removing unproductive time. The 47% would then have to work through something else, such as fewer interruptions or less fragmented case time. That is plausible, but it is a different mechanism from the one the nine-month report proposed.
- One sentence defining what the log measure includes would resolve this.

**4. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**
- The effective sample is 14 offices. "A larger sample of office-months" adds precision only if errors are clustered by office. Were they? A 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow for seven treated offices.
- The mediators were not randomised. Reverse causation is plausible: better-run offices may cut meetings and produce more.
- The plan was registered at month 11, when meeting data up to that point had been partly seen. The outcomes were still unknown, so this is a minor issue, but it is worth stating.
- The ranking of meetings above fatigue is plausible, but the intervals (28–66 and 2–34) touch.
- "Supports a substantial meetings pathway" fits the evidence. "Confirms 47%" does not. The limitations section already concedes the confounding problem; the summary should match it.

**5. The Halden subset figure is favourable, but not a bound.**
- The selection is triple, not double: submitting records, responding (14 of 23), then continuing.
- With no comparison group, trends affecting the wider economy over the two years could push the figure either way. "Likely favourable estimate" is accurate; "upper bound" is not guaranteed.
- One reversion was a marketing agency, which would usually be coded as discretionary work, citing client deadlines. Discretionary work can be deadline-bound too. The binary coding of work type in the meta-analysis misses this, and it deserves a sentence.

**6. Smaller points**
- **Cost per contact.** If 12% more staff restored contacts to control levels, staff cost per contact would rise about 12%. The 9% figure presumably includes non-staff costs or a residual per-hour gain. Showing the derivation would help.
- **Sick days.** The question I raised about the earlier papers is still open: if the shorter week means fewer working days, absence per FTE falls mechanically. Report sick days per scheduled day.
- **"Since dismissed as post hoc".** Only Varga & Holm dismissed the meetings pathway. The meta-analysis said it could not be assessed.

# Where the evidence now stands

| Status | Finding |
|---|---|
| Found | In discretionary public-sector case work, a randomised two-year comparison with record-based output shows a per-hour gain of about 8–10%. The gain is not an artifact. |
| Found | In the same work, output per employee is slightly below control: about −3%, with a CI that includes zero. The hours cut is mostly, not fully, offset. |
| Found | In coverage-bound work, reduced hours cost service and require more staff. The county ended the arm. |
| Supported, not settled | Cutting meetings is a substantial part of the mechanism. Fatigue contributes less. About a third of the gain is unexplained. |
| Open | Whether the gain decays. It persisted at 24 months, but the decline has not been tested and may be inflated by the control-arm audit. |
| Open | Whether reorganising without cutting hours captures most of the gain. Only two uncontrolled offices bear on this, and no arm tested it. |
| Open | Generalisation beyond one public employer, beyond 24 months, and to private discretionary work with client deadlines. |

The most valuable next step follows from the last two rows: a trial with a third arm that cuts meetings at full hours.

I can draft the decomposition analysis for point 2, or a design for that three-arm trial.
